Stir Up the Gift
STUR UP the GIFT
v. phrase
From Paul's charge to Timothy, anazopyrein to charisma, to rekindle into flame the gift; Greek anazopyreō (to fan into flame) and charisma (gift of grace), in 2 Tim 1:6.

Biblical Definition

To Stir Up the Gift is the apostolic charge laid upon the minister to kindle, exercise, and diligently improve the spiritual gift God has bestowed on him for his office. Paul writes to Timothy: "Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands" (2 Tim 1:6). The verb is anazopyreō, to fan a fire into fresh flame—a vivid figure: the gift is like coals which, though never extinguished, may grow dim and sluggish through neglect, and must be stirred and blown upon that they may blaze again. The charisma here is the ministerial gifting conferred upon Timothy for the work of the evangelist and pastor, attested by the laying on of the presbytery's hands (1 Tim 4:14), comprehending the abilities for preaching, teaching, and oversight. The charge implies two truths. First, the gift is God's gift, sovereignly bestowed; the minister does not generate it but receives it. Second, the gift is given to be used, and the responsibility to employ it diligently rests upon the man who has it. Paul therefore presses the same point: "Neglect not the gift that is in thee" (1 Tim 4:14), and "give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine... meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them" (1 Tim 4:13, 15). The charge stands against ministerial sloth, that besetting sin which lets gifts lie buried like the wicked servant's talent, that grows cold in study, slack in prayer, and perfunctory in preaching. As cessationist, this dictionary does not regard the gift in view as a continuing sign-gift such as tongues or healing, but as the abiding gifts of teaching, exhortation, and rule that Christ still gives His church through her ministers. This dictionary confesses that every man entrusted with a gift for Christ's service is bound to stir it up, to fan it into flame by diligent use, prayer, and meditation, lest by sloth he bury what God has given for the good of His people.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines to STIR UP as to incite, instigate, or rouse to action; and GIFT as a present or endowment bestowed. To Stir Up the Gift is to rouse and diligently exercise the ministerial gifting God has bestowed (2 Tim 1:6).

expand to see more

STIR, v.t. — To excite; to instigate; to prompt; to rouse into action; as, to stir up the embers of a fire, or to stir up the mind.

GIFT, n. — A present; a thing given or bestowed; the act of giving; the right or power of giving; also, the faculty or power bestowed; an endowment.

"Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands" (2 Tim 1:6).

It requires the diligent kindling and exercise of the gift through study, prayer, and use; it forbids the sloth and neglect that lets the gift grow cold and dim.

The gift is God's sovereign bestowal, yet given to be improved—the minister must fan it into flame lest he bury it like the wicked servant's talent.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 1:6 — "Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands."

1 Timothy 4:14 — "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery."

1 Timothy 4:15 — "Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all."

Matthew 25:25 — "And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine."

Modern Corruption

The charge to Stir Up the Gift confronts ministerial sloth and neglect—the burying of God-given gifts through coldness in study, prayer, and labor—and warns against presuming on a gift while failing to exercise it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger this charge addresses is not a modern redefinition but the perennial sin of sloth in the Lord's servants. The man entrusted with a gift for Christ's service may, through ease, discouragement, or the press of lesser things, let his gift grow dim—coals that smoulder for want of stirring. His study grows shallow, his prayers brief, his preaching mechanical, until the gift that once blazed gives little light or heat. Against this Paul charges Timothy to fan the gift into flame (2 Tim 1:6) and to neglect it not (1 Tim 4:14). The positive principle to recover is diligent improvement: the minister is bound to give attendance to reading, exhortation, and doctrine, to meditate upon these things and give himself wholly to them, that his profiting may appear to all.

A related abuse is presumption upon the gift without its exercise—the man who, conscious of real ability, trusts the gift to carry him and so labors little, neglecting the means by which the gift is kept bright. But gifts unimproved are gifts despised, and the parable of the talents warns that the servant who buries what his lord entrusted is called wicked and slothful, and what he has is taken from him (Matt 25:25-29). The recovery is to hold gift and diligence together: the gift is God's, freely given and not earned; yet it is given to be used, and the steward is accountable to improve it with all diligence, prayer, and labor, for the good of the church and the glory of the Giver. To stir up the gift is no optional fervor but a binding charge upon all whom Christ has gifted for His service.

Hebrew Roots

The charge rests on Paul's anazopyrein to charisma tou theou (2 Tim 1:6), to fan into flame the gift of God—the diligent kindling of ministerial gifting against sloth.

expand to see more

Greek anazopyreō (G329) — to rekindle, fan into flame; the vivid verb of 2 Tim 1:6, the gift stirred like coals into fresh fire.

Greek charisma (G5486) — gift of grace; the ministerial endowment God bestows for the work of His service.

Greek ameleō (G272) — to neglect, be careless of; the verb forbidden in 1 Tim 4:14, "neglect not the gift."

Greek meletō (G3191) — to meditate, attend to, practise; the diligent attendance commanded in 1 Tim 4:15.

The gift is God's sovereign bestowal, yet given to be improved, and the steward is bound to fan it into flame by diligent use.

Usage

"Paul charged Timothy to Stir Up the Gift of God that was in him, lest it grow cold through neglect."

"Wearied by long labor, the old pastor resolved afresh to Stir Up the Gift, giving himself wholly to reading, prayer, and doctrine."

"To Stir Up the Gift is no optional fervor but a binding charge against the sloth that buries what God has given."
